metadata.title: Best Punjabi-Banarasi Winter Home Food I Kaanji, Gajar Matar, Methi Aloo, Gobhi Aloo, Gajar Halwa
metadata.description:
Delhi is a melting pot of cultures, where every household carries its own unique culinary traditions. Each community weaves a different story through the food they cook, and within those communities, every family adds its own touch. This is what led us to start Community Food Stories—an initiative to bring you the warmth, nostalgia and love found in home kitchens.  

In today’s episode, we step into the home of chef-turned-food entrepreneur Kishi Arora, where her mother, Kanan Bala Ji, welcomes us with a Punjabi-Banarasi winter feast. A passionate home chef who finds pure joy in feeding people, she brings together the bold, comforting flavours of Punjab and the nuanced influences of Benaras, where she spent her early years. Through her Instagram page, Mamakeats, she has been sharing these cherished family recipes, keeping traditions alive with every dish.  

Our day began with Kanan Ji walking us through some of the family’s favourite winter dishes. She started with baby aloo methi and a lesser-known seasonal delicacy, kalattar ki sabzi—a dish made from tender pea peels, cooked simply with a few spices to let the freshness shine. Alongside, she prepared gajar matar ki sabzi, another winter favourite that celebrates the best of the season’s produce.  

As the kitchen filled with comforting aromas, she introduced us to a dish close to her heart—bathua ka raita, a winter specialty that adds a refreshing balance to the meal. Gobi aloo and chole had been prepared earlier, setting the stage for the final, much-awaited touch—puffed, golden masala pooris. The plate came together in a beautiful burst of colors and flavours. The richness of flavours was elevated by the love of a mother’s hands.  

Between cooking, we took a walk through Kishi’s lush terrace garden, a space that breathes life into their meals. Overflowing with fresh herbs and vegetables, it’s a sanctuary of homegrown goodness.  

No winter feast is complete without dessert, and gajar ka halwa was the perfect indulgence. This halwa wasn’t rushed—it had been slow-cooked for 18 hours, allowing the flavors to deepen. Every bite was a taste of patience and love.  

Later in the afternoon, Kanan Ji treated us to another winter specialty—matar chura, a dish inspired by Benaras. Unlike the usual poha, this version has a higher proportion of fresh green peas, flavoured with warming spices and a hint of sugar. It was a simple yet delightful snack, bringing together the warmth and sweetness of winter’s bounty.  

This was more than just a food experience—it was a celebration of traditions, memories, and the joy of sharing a meal with loved ones. As we wrapped up the day, we left with full hearts and an even deeper appreciation for home-cooked meals. The warmth of Kishi’s family made this experience truly special.
